question: What is the maximum administrative fine for infringing the basic principles for processing, including the conditions for consent?
answer: Up to 20 000 000 EUR, or in the case of an undertaking, up to 4 % of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (GDPR p. 83, Article 83(5)). Up to 10 000 000 EUR, or in the case of an undertaking, up to 2 % of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (GDPR p. 82, Article 83(4)).
cited: GDPR p. 83, Article 83(5); GDPR p. 82, Article 83(4)

question: Up to what amount can a company be fined for infringing the obligations of the controller and the processor under Articles 8, 11, 25 to 39, 42 and 43?
answer: Up to 10 000 000 EUR, or in the case of an undertaking, up to 2 % of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (GDPR p. 82, Article 83(4)).

question: Within how many hours must a controller notify a personal data breach to the supervisory authority?
answer: The controller shall without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority (GDPR p. 52, Article 33(1)). Where the notification to the supervisory authority is not made within 72 hours, it shall be accompanied by reasons for the delay (GDPR p. 52, Article 33(1)).
cited: GDPR p. 52, Article 33(1); GDPR p. 52, Article 33(1)

question: How does the GDPR define the consent of the data subject?
answer: Consent is any freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication of the data subject's wishes (GDPR p. 34, Article 4(11)). Consent should be given by a clear affirmative act (GDPR p. 6, Recital (32)). Silence, pre-ticked boxes or inactivity should not constitute consent (GDPR p. 6, Recital (32)). Consent should cover all processing activities carried out for the same purpose or purposes (GDPR p. 6, Recital (32)).
cited: GDPR p. 34, Article 4(11); GDPR p. 6, Recital (32); GDPR p. 6, Recital (32); GDPR p. 6, Recital (32)

question: From what age can a child consent on their own to information society services under the GDPR, and how low may Member States set that age?
answer: The processing of the personal data of a child shall be lawful where the child is at least 16 years old (GDPR p. 37, Article 8(1)). Member States may provide by law for a lower age for those purposes provided that such lower age is not below 13 years (GDPR p. 37, Article 8(1)).
cited: GDPR p. 37, Article 8(1); GDPR p. 37, Article 8(1)

question: How quickly must a controller respond to a data subject's request, and can that period be extended?
answer: The controller shall provide information on action taken on a request under Articles 15 to 22 to the data subject without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt of the request (GDPR p. 40, Article 12(3)). That period may be extended by two further months where necessary, taking into account the complexity and number of the requests (GDPR p. 40, Article 12(3)).
cited: GDPR p. 40, Article 12(3); GDPR p. 40, Article 12(3)

question: From which date does the GDPR apply?
answer: From 25 May 2018 (GDPR pp. 87-88, Article 99(2)).

question: When must a controller or processor designate a data protection officer?
answer: The controller and the processor shall designate a data protection officer in any case where (GDPR p. 55, Article 37(1)). In cases other than those referred to in paragraph 1, the controller or processor or associations and other bodies representing categories of controllers or processors may or, where required by Union or Member State law shall, designate a data protection officer (GDPR p. 55, Article 37(4)).
cited: GDPR p. 55, Article 37(1); GDPR p. 55, Article 37(4)

question: Under the ePrivacy Directive, on what condition may information be stored in or read from a user's terminal equipment, such as cookies?
answer: On condition that the subscriber or user concerned is provided with clear and comprehensive information in accordance with Directive 95/46/EC, inter alia about the purposes of the processing, and is offered the right to refuse such processing by the data controller (ePrivacy p. 8, Article 5(3)). Users should have the opportunity to refuse to have a cookie or similar device stored on their terminal equipment (ePrivacy p. 3, Recital (25)).
cited: ePrivacy p. 8, Article 5(3); ePrivacy p. 3, Recital (25)

question: Under the ePrivacy Directive, what must happen to traffic data once it is no longer needed for transmitting a communication?
answer: Traffic data must be erased or made anonymous when it is no longer needed for the purpose of the transmission of a communication (ePrivacy p. 8, Article 6(1)). This does not conflict with caching procedures on the Internet (ePrivacy p. 4, Recital (28)).
cited: ePrivacy p. 8, Article 6(1); ePrivacy p. 4, Recital (28)

question: Under the ePrivacy Directive, may a company send marketing e-mails to its existing customers without asking for consent again?
answer: The company may use the electronic contact details for direct marketing of similar products or services provided that customers clearly and distinctly are given the opportunity to object (ePrivacy p. 9, Article 13(2)). The company must inform the customer about the further use for direct marketing in a clear and distinct manner, and be given the opportunity to refuse such usage (ePrivacy p. 6, Recital (41)).
cited: ePrivacy p. 9, Article 13(2); ePrivacy p. 6, Recital (41)

question: Within how many hours must a personal data breach be notified to the supervisory authority, and when must the affected data subjects also be informed?
answer: Notification to the supervisory authority must be made without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it (GDPR p. 52, Article 33(1); GDPR pp. 16-17, Recital (85)). Affected data subjects should be informed of the existence of the processing operation and its purposes, and other necessary information (GDPR p. 12, Recital (60); GDPR p. 12, Recital (61)).
cited: GDPR p. 52, Article 33(1); GDPR pp. 16-17, Recital (85); GDPR p. 12, Recital (60); GDPR p. 12, Recital (61)

question: The ePrivacy Directive defines consent by reference to Directive 95/46/EC. Which act do such references point to today, and how does that act define consent?
answer: The ePrivacy Directive references Directive 95/46/EC for the definition of consent (ePrivacy p. 7, Article 2; ePrivacy p. 2, Recital (17)). The ePrivacy Directive references Directive 95/46/EC for the definition of consent, [C1] (ePrivacy p. 7, Article 2).
cited: ePrivacy p. 7, Article 2; ePrivacy p. 2, Recital (17); ePrivacy p. 7, Article 2

question: Does the GDPR impose additional obligations on providers of public electronic communications services, and what does the ePrivacy Directive require for traffic data that is no longer needed?
answer: GDPR does not impose additional obligations on providers of public electronic communications services (GDPR p. 86, Article 95). Traffic data must be erased or made anonymous when it is no longer needed for the purpose of the transmission of a communication (ePrivacy p. 8, Article 6(1)).
cited: GDPR p. 86, Article 95; ePrivacy p. 8, Article 6(1)

question: What fine applies when a company does not comply with an order of the supervisory authority, and how does it compare with the fine for infringing the controller's obligations under Article 25 to 39?
answer: The fine for non-compliance with an order of the supervisory authority is up to 20,000,000 EUR, or 4% of the total worldwide annual turnover (GDPR p. 83, Article 83(6)). The fine for infringing the controller's obligations under Article 25 to 39 is up to 10,000,000 EUR, or 2% of the total worldwide annual turnover (GDPR p. 82, Article 83(4)).
cited: GDPR p. 83, Article 83(6); GDPR p. 82, Article 83(4)
